title: Castling, and when you cannot
outcomes: Knows the four conditions and which attacked squares matter
Spots when castling is not available

steps.text: You just **castled**: the king slid two squares toward a rook, and that rook jumped to the king's other side. Toward the h-file is **kingside** (written O-O), toward the a-file is **queenside** (O-O-O). Castling tucks the king away and brings a rook into play. It is never forced: you castle only when you want to.

steps.caption: Kingside: the king goes two squares and the rook hops to its other side.

line.say: The king goes two squares toward the rook, and the rook jumps over it to the square beside the king.

steps.caption: Queenside: the king still goes two squares, but the rook travels three.

line.say: The king goes two squares toward the a-file, and the rook jumps over it to d1.

steps.text:
Castling is allowed only when **all four** are true.
1. The king and that rook have never moved (a moved king ends castling on both sides; a moved rook only on its own side).
2. Every square between them is empty.
3. The king is not in check right now.
4. The king does not cross or land on an attacked square.
Squares only the rook crosses do not matter. Here is one failure of each.

steps.caption: Condition 1. A king that went out and came back. Castling is gone for good: the game remembers a king that has moved.

claims.statement: White can no longer castle toward the h-file.
White can no longer castle toward the a-file.

steps.caption: Condition 2. The knight on b1 stands between king and rook, so castling toward the a-file is illegal until it leaves.

line.say: The knight steps out of the way, so b1 is empty.
Black makes a quiet move. Now b1, c1 and d1 are all empty.

claims.statement: Castling toward the a-file is blocked at first.
Castling toward the h-file is already legal.

steps.caption: Condition 3. The rook gives check, so castling is off. White must answer the check some other way.

line.say: The king steps off the e-file. That is a legal way to answer the check.

claims.statement: Castling toward the h-file is not allowed in check.
Castling toward the a-file is not allowed in check.

steps.caption: Condition 4. The rook on f3 attacks f1, a square the king would cross: kingside is off, queenside is fine.
b1 is attacked by the bishop, but only the rook crosses it, so castling toward the a-file is still legal.

steps.text: **Model answer.** Castling moves the king two squares toward a rook and the rook jumps to the king's other side, for either colour, kingside or queenside. It needs: king and rook never moved, nothing between them, no check now, and no attacked square on the king's route. It is a choice, never a duty.

steps.prompt: Read the model answer, cover it, then explain castling in your own words and name the condition you are most likely to forget.
